blocks.text: To these must be added the famous passage on the eagle in Iob. XXXIX, 27. var. 30., in which God addresses his servant thus: Will the eagle rise up at your command, and set her nest on high? She dwells on the rock, and on the sheer crag as in a citadel she abides. From there she searches out food, her eyes gazing far off; and her chicks suck up blood; and where the slain are, there is she. Since all of this pertains to the nature of the eagle, it must be expounded carefully. Will the eagle, he says, rise up at your command? namely in lofty flight. Man did not give the eagle this nature, that she should rise up to the very clouds; nor can you steer her in flight and bend her to your will, since at times she is so high in the air that she wholly escapes the sight of men. At your command, etc. will she set her nest on high in places that are often impassable and inaccessible to us? This the following words explain thus: She dwells on the rock, and on the sheer crag as in a citadel she abides. The Septuagint: Ἐπ᾽ ἐξοχῇ πέτρας, καὶ ἀποκρύφῳ [Ep᾽ exochē petras, kai apokryphō]. Had they not rather written καὶ ἀποκρήμνῳ [kai apokrēmnō]? So Jerome: She remains on the rocks, she lingers on sheer flints and on inaccessible cliffs. Not very differently the Philosopher, on the nests of eagles, Histor. book 9, ch. 32: Ποιοῦνται δὲ αὐτὰς οὐκ ἐν πεδινοῖς τόποις, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν ὑψηλοῖς μάλιστα μὲν, καὶ ἐν πέτραις ἀποκρήμνοις· [Poiountai de autas ouk en pedinois topois, all᾽ en hypsēlois malista men, kai en petrais apokrēmnois] They make them not in level places but in lofty ones, and chiefly on sheer cliffs. And Pliny, book 10, ch. 3: They nest on rocks. And Damir, in the chapter On النسر [al-nasr] or the Eagle: تبيض في الاماكن [tabīḍu fī al-amākin] [II, 755] العالية [al-ʿāliya] She lays her eggs in lofty places ^{(3)}. And in the chapter On العقاب [al-ʿuqāb] alokab, or the Melanaeetus: ولا تقعد الا علي الاماكن المرتفعة [wa-lā taqʿudu illā ʿalī al-amākin al-murtafiʿa] She dwells only in elevated places. As Pliny says of the same bird: It keeps to the mountains. And Albertus of the herodius, the name by which barbarous writers call the larger eagle: It is always found sitting and nesting on sheer flints.

There are, moreover, two reasons why she betakes herself to these steep places, which the sacred writer touches on here in passing. The first, that they may serve her as מצודה, that is, as ὀχυρώματος [ochyrōmatos], or a stronghold, as Aquila rightly rendered it; and that the chicks, which she is forced to leave in the nest in order to provide food for them, may be safe by the very nature of the place. For such lofty crags are not open to just anyone. To this pertains what the Arabs relate in Damir: قيل لبشار بن يزد الاعمي الشاعر لو خيرك الله أن تكون حيوانا ماذا كنت تختار قال العقاب لانها تلبث حيث لا يبلغها سبع ولا ذواريع وتحيد عنها سباع الطير [qīla li-Bashshār ibn Yazd al-aʿmī al-shāʿir law khayyaraka Allāh an takūna ḥayawānan mādhā kunta takhtār qāla al-ʿuqāb li-annahā talbathu ḥaythu lā yablughuhā sabʿ wa-lā dhawārīʿ wa-taḥīdu ʿanhā sibāʿ al-ṭayr] Besar, son of Iazid, the blind poet, when asked what he would choose if God gave him the option of becoming any animal, answered: Alokab (that is, that he would choose the melanaeetus), because it dwells in places inaccessible to all wild beasts and animals, and even the birds of prey flee from meeting it.

The second reason why the eagle prefers to dwell in a lofty place is expressed thus in Job: [col. 174] From there she searches out food, her eyes gazing far off. Nor did this escape the Philosopher, who says of the eagle in the place cited above: Ὑψοῦ δὲ πέτεται, ὅπως ἐπὶ πλεῖστον τόπον καθορᾷ [Hypsou de petetai, hopōs epi pleiston topon kathora], She flies high, so as to look down upon more places. And Apuleius: When therefore the eagle has borne herself up there, etc. looking down upon everything from there, etc. she gazes around and seeks where above all she should swoop down from on high upon her prey. These things agree with the words of Job: From there she searches out food, her eyes looking down from afar. Searches out is in Hebrew חפר, a verb which properly means to dig, but here to search out with the eyes. The same kind of metaphor is found in the verb rimari [to search out]. For properly rimari is rimas agere [to make cracks], and almost the same as fodere [to dig]. Hence the Poet in book 3 of the Georgics:

So with difficulty they scratch the earth with hoes, and with their very nails dig in the grain. — — — [II, 756] Nor is it added in vain that the eagle gazes far off with her eyes. For no animal is more sharp-sighted than the eagle. Homer, Iliad ρ΄ [17], line 674:
— — — ὥς τ᾽ αἰετὸς, ὅν ῥά τέ φασιν Ὀξύτατον δέρκεσθαι ὑπουρανίων πετεηνῶν. [hōs t᾽ aietos, hon rha te phasin Oxytaton derkesthai hypouraniōn peteēnōn]

Like the eagle, which they say sees most keenly of the birds of the air. Where the Scholiast says: Αἰετός· ὄρνις δορατικὸς (an legendum διορατικὸς) καὶ ὀξὺς ἐν τῷ ὁρᾷν, καὶ ἵπτασθαι [Aietos· ornis doratikos (or should we read dioratikos) kai oxys en tō horan, kai hiptasthai]. Aelian likewise, Hist. book 1, ch. 42: Αἰετὸς δὲ ὀρνίθων ὀξυωπήστερος [Aietos de ornithōn oxyōpēsteros]. Horace, Serm. 1, Sat. 3:
— — — — you see as sharply as either the eagle or the Epidaurian serpent.
